blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Shor's 1996 breakthrough paper as a 'Great moment in computing,' demonstrating that quantum computers can efficiently factor primes—a task with profound implications for cryptography. The blog post emphasizes the algorithm's significance, noting its first real-world execution in 2001 (factoring 15) and the challenge of understanding the paper's dense presentation. Colyer points to accessible explanations by Scott Aaronson and Kelsey Houston-Edward to clarify the algorithm's mechanics. Beyond the algorithm itself, the post explores the broader question of which problems quantum computers can solve efficiently, contrasting classical complexity classes (P, NP, NP-complete) with quantum complexity (BQP). It concludes that Shor's algorithm is a canonical example of a problem (factoring integers and discrete logarithms) where quantum computers outperform classical ones, leveraging superposition and interference to exploit global solution-space properties.
paper_title: Polynomial-time algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms on a quantum computer
paper_abstract: A digital computer is generally believed to be an efficient universal computing device; that is, it is believed able to simulate any physical computing device with an increase in computation time by at most a polynomial factor. This may not be true when quantum mechanics is taken into consideration. This paper considers factoring integers and finding discrete logarithms, two problems which are generally thought to be hard on a classical computer and which have been used as the basis of several proposed cryptosystems. Efficient randomized algorithms are given for these two problems on a hypothetical quantum computer. These algorithms take a number of steps polynomial in the input size, e.g., the number of digits of the integer to be factored.
